# Declarative vs imperative:

In declarative, you need to tell what you want, not how you want to achieve it. Like HTML or SQL.  
In imperative, you need to tell how; like Python or C.  
Functional programming is a kind of declarative programming in which the program will have nested functions, each of them get the output statelessly to the outer function.

The identifier of an object is retrieved using id(). It’s the object’s memory address.  
Operand is something that the operation is being done on. Operator is something that does the operation.  
2+3  
2 and 3 are operands.  
Ternary operators: if, else  
Unary operators: \+, \-  
Binary operators: \=, \<  
We have complex numbers in python: 3+4j for example  
// is floor division. 12 // 5 result 2  
Division will always give a float.

match/case:  
my\_operation \= "read"   
match my\_operation:   
    case "read":   
        print("perform read operation…")   
    case "update":   
        print("perform update operation …")   
    case "insert":   
        print("perform insert operation …")   
    case "delete":   
        print("perform delete operation …")   
    case \_:   
        print("wrong variant if operation \!\!\!")

Ternary expression:  
is\_apple \= "Yes" if fruit \== "apple" else "No"

**In Python, everything can be converted to bool**

**With the while loop, you can also use the else operator to run some code once when the condition is no longer True. also it can be used for one step after for, when the loop is finished.**

**While loop runs while the condition expression is True**

Carriage return will remove whatever comes before it

Strings can be sliced using slice() function:

slice(\[start\], \[stop\], \[step\])

my\_str \= "Hello"

slice\_object \= slice(1, 3\)

print(my\_str\[slice\_object\])

You can also write it like string\[start:stop:step\]. Step of \-1 will reverse the order.

Look at this code:  
b, a \= a, b

This way, you are packing and unpacking the variables and swap them without a temporary value.

“Is” checks the memory address to be the same, not the value. “==” checks the value.

Sets have “union” (like union in math). You can use it like this:  
set 1 | set2 | set3

Or

set1.union(set2, set3)

Just like that, you can use intersections:

set 1 & set2 & set3

Or

set1.intersection(set2, set3)

And difference:

set 1 \- set2 \- set3

Or

set1.difference(set2, set3)

![][image1]

The update method changes the value of the original set to the union with the specified sets. Like extend in list.

The intersection\_update and the difference\_update methods work similarly, but with intersection and difference, respectively.

Add and remove methods are like append and remove in list. They add and remove elements from set. We also have clear method which removes everything from the list.

Hashing is something fun. All immutable objects are hashable; but only some of mutable objects are hashable.

Hash maps are dicts in python. The time complexity of finding a hash value by its key is O(1). However sometimes we have one hash for two keys and we call it collisions. We have to handle it. This is why sometimes dicts’ complexity is O(n) instead of O(1).

What is a first class entity?

It’s something that you can do whatever you want with it. So functions are first class:

- You can assign them to a variable  
- You can pass them as a function argument  
- You can put them inside data structures  
- You can return them

This is weird:

(pos1, pos2, /, pos\_or\_kwd1, pos\_or\_kwd2='default', \*args,kwd\_only1, kwd\_only2='default', \*\*kwargs):

So important:

In python, immutable objects are passed to the functions by value. But mutable objects are passed by reference (**wow\!\!**). This is why IDE warns you when you give mutable objects as default value of an argument. If you call such a function 2 times, the object inside the function will persist after the first call.

kwd\_only1, kwd\_only2='default', \*\*kwargs)

Some design concepts:

Coupling: 

1. Keep the function isolated from outside world. It should just get the inputs and give an output  
2. Don’t change mutable args unless the function logic requires you to.

Cohesion:

1. Functions have a single purpose that can be expressed in a simple sentence with no conjunction.

Lambda syntax:

Lambda arg1, arg2, …, argN: \<statement\>

Map:

Returns an iterator that applies function on each item of the iterable:

map(function, iterable)

Filter:

Just like map, but if the function returns true.

Reduce:

This is interesting. It takes the first two items of the iterable, applies the function to them, then takes the output of the function and the third item and applies the function to them and recursively does that until only one item is left. reduce(lambda x, y: x+y, \[1, 2, 3, 4, 5\]) calculates ((((1+2)+3)+4)+5)s

It also gets an initializer value to be used as the first item:

reduce(function, iterable, initial\_value)

Recursion:

Recursions can always be written as loops and vice versa.

For recursion we should have a base case (or exit condition), and recursive case which is calling the function itself with a modified argument.

Namespace:

Name spaces are places in which the values are stored. Namespaces are implemented as dictionaries. Keys are object names and values are the objects.

We have four namespaces:

- Builtin: created when the interpreter starts, terminates when interpreter is closed  
- Global: the namespace of the main program or when you import something. It will terminate when the interpreter is closed. We can have multiple global namespaces, each of them for a different module.  
- Enclosing: for the function that has another function inside  
- Local: for functions just exists when the function is running with no function inside

After termination, the memory might take time to be freed. But the references will be invalid.

The interpreter looks foreach name from inside out: local, then inclosing, then global, then builtin. This is LEGB rule.

Scope:

Scope is “how” to find a value in the namespace.

Builtin namespace doesn’t behave like a dictionary. Python implements it as a module. However, global and local dictionaries are really dictionaries. To access them, you can use globals() and locals() functions. You can also edit the variables using globals() but not locals(); like a dictionary:

globals()\[‘a’\] \= 2 \#this is like a=2

You remember that a dictionary is a hashmap. So we can say that Python has different hashmaps which map the variable names (references) to their objects. Also remember about the mutable data types. They can be modified outside of their scope.

“global” in python is like global in java. You can access global variables inside the function even if you haven’t used them as an argument. Also, you can use globals() dictionary to create or modify global variables in other scopes.

“nonlocal” is like global, but it is used to access the variable from an outer function (enclosing) in the local namespace.

But, better not to use nonlocal and global.

Decorator:

These allow us to modify the function behaviour without altering its code. They take the func as an arg. So you can pass a function to a decorator, then the return value will be a wrapped function which is different. So we have a wrapper function, which adds functionalities around the arged function. Then we have a decorator, which returns this wrapper. The wrapper doesn’t get the function as input; decorator does.

def my\_decorator(function\_to\_decorate): 

    def wrapper\_around\_original\_function(): 

        print("I am a code running before the original function.") 

        function\_to\_decorate() 

        print("And I am the code that runs after")

decorated\_function \= my\_decorator(function\_to\_decorate)

decorated\_function()

This can be written like:

@my\_decorator

def function\_to\_decorate():

    statements

Decorators could be nested.

coffee \= sugar(milk(coffee))

Is just like:

@sugar

@milk

def coffee(variety="arabica"):

    print(variety)

The order is important here.

    return wrapper\_around\_original\_function

Modules:

You can write the modules in C/C++ in case of using Cython or Java in case of using Jython. 

You can define “\_\_all\_\_” variable in the init function and then you can specify which variables are available for importing from the module.

PYTHONPATH can be set to search for additional directories for finding modules.

Sys.path gives you the paths python look for modules.

\_\_name\_\_ is the module name when you import it, but it is \_\_main\_\_ when you are executing it.

If you want to do circular import, import them inside functions.

All code in \_\_init\_\_ will be executed when importing.

# OOP:

* Polymorphism:  
* Using a single signature for different types.  
  * Ad hoc: a function that can accept arguments with different types and behave differently based on the type  
  * Parametric: functions will operate on different types without the need to specify their types  
* issubclass(cls, class\_or\_tuple) is like isinstance(cls, class\_or\_tuple).  
* One underscore before the attribute name means it is protected (only class and subclasses have access). \_protected\_attr. You can access them using: obj.\_attributeName  
* Two means it is private (only the class has access). \_\_private\_attr. You can access them using: obj.\_ClassName\_\_attributeName  
* Diamond problem: When a class inherits from 2 classes, and they have the same parent. If for example, there is a function in both of these with the same name, which one will the child inherit?  
* method resolution order (MRO): the way the child in the diamond problem chooses the function to call. In resolving the function, the classes will be searched from bottom to top and from left to right.  
  ![][image2]  
* The order will be determined using C3 linearization.

## Class decorators:

### @classmethod:

Class methods don’t take “self” but “cls”. So they don’t talk to instances themselves but the classes.  They modify the state of the class.

### @staticmethod:

They wont take cls or self as arg and they can be called before instantiation.

### @property:

A method with property decorator is a property of the class. In other words it’s a field, which is dynamic like a method, but it doesn’t need to be called like a method. It can be treated like a property.

class Person:   
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, first\_name, last\_name):   
        self.first\_name \= first\_name   
        self.last\_name \= last\_name   
   
    @property   
    def email(self):   
        return f"{self.first\_name}.{self.last\_name}@email.com"   
\>\>\> obj \= Person("Alex", "Johnson")   
\>\>\> obj.email   
'Alex.Johnson@email.com'   
\>\>\> obj.first\_name \= "Bob"   
\>\>\> obj.email   
'Bob.Johnson@email.com'

## ABC (abstract class):

Should has at least @abstractmethod or @abstractclass otherwise will be a regular class. These methods and properties should be overridden on the child classes or else we will get type error.

## Exception handling:

else: This comes after except. If the error is not caught, it will execute its statement.  
finally: like in java. You can close the resources even if the error is not caught with finally.

## Magic methods:

### \_\_call\_\_()

As you know, functions are objects. But they are callable, meaning that they have this method implemented in them. So if you want your class to be callable, add this method to it.

### 

### \_\_iter\_\_(), \_\_next\_\_()

Look at this:

class Repeat:  
   def \_\_init\_\_(self, msg):  
     self.msg \= msg  
       
   def \_\_iter\_\_(self):  
     return self  
       
   def \_\_next\_\_(self):  
     return self.msg

A for loop like this:

obj \= Repeat("car")  
for message in obj:  
   print(message)

Is just this:

obj \= Repeat("car")  
obj\_iterator \= obj.\_\_iter\_\_()  
while True:  
  message \= obj\_iterator.\_\_next\_\_()  
  print(message)

Context manager:  
When you call “with”, you are actually calling \_\_init\_\_(), \_\_enter\_\_() and \_\_exit\_\_() methods.  
You call the init, then enter. After that you finish the task you want and call exit. Exit should have self, exc\_type, exc\_val, exc\_tb .If during the execution an exception happens, the args exc\_type, exc\_val, exc\_tb will hold its type, value and traceback.  
Enter should return self

# Descriptors:

These are classes with \_\_set\_\_, \_\_get\_\_ and \_\_delete\_\_ that add dynamicity to the attributes.  
You can add dynamicity to \_\_init\_\_ but later on, you will not be able to do the same when assigning values to them.   
These functions’ signature is like this:  
\_\_get\_\_(self, obj, type=None)      
\_\_set\_\_(self, obj, value)

Here are the argument descriptions:

- self: the descriptor instance  
- obj: the instance of the class that the descriptor is attached to  
- type: the type of the object the descriptor is attached to
